artifacts.synopsis: A ruling elder appealed convictions and censures arising from his brief refusal to leave a closed Temporary Session meeting. The SJC affirmed only his conviction for failing to submit to church government, because he knowingly attended and his apology acknowledged fault; it reversed findings of dereliction, sedition, rioting, and the balance for lack of supporting evidence. It rejected his first four appeal specifications, but held suspension and deposition excessive, substituted Admonition, and restored both sacraments and office, although he belonged to no particular Session.

artifacts.title: Doty v. Nashville Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: A complainant challenged Nashville Presbytery's handling of allegations against a teaching elder. The SJC held the matter judicially out of order and dismissed it, finding the original filing with the church session was not a BCO 43-1 complaint because the session lacked jurisdiction over the teaching elder. Presbytery properly treated the allegations as BCO 31-2/34-1 reports, and the complainant, not a Nashville member, lacked standing to complain about that new action. A nine-member dissent argued the filing of charges conferred standing under prior SJC cases.

artifacts.synopsis: Hahn challenged Presbytery’s ruling that CTKPC Session lawfully excluded him from that congregation’s worship until a psychiatric evaluation addressed safety concerns. The SJC denied the complaint. Applying BCO 39-3.3, it found no clear error in the lower courts’ credibility and discretionary judgments, given Session’s familiarity with the people and events. It characterized the restriction as informal pastoral safety guidance, not judicial discipline: it did not bar sacraments, worship elsewhere, or transfer, and attendance could resume upon medical assurance. The conditional local restriction therefore remained undisturbed.

artifacts.title: Lee v. Korean Eastern Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: Korean Eastern Presbytery dismissed TE Eliot Lee's charges against two teaching elders without trial, and the SJC sustained Lee's complaint that this was unconstitutional. Although a presbytery may dismiss charges under BCO 29-1, 32-20, 34-2, or 31-8, it bears the burden of documenting that basis; KEP did not. The SJC refused Lee's request that it enter the guilt verdicts the presbytery should have reached—that power exists on appeal, not complaint. It remanded for KEP to begin process under BCO 32.
